---
title: "Self-check: transfer the reasoning"
---

Answer before opening each explanation. Draw where appropriate; a correct label
without a chemical explanation is only a starting point. These are formative checks.

## 1. What is the stereocentre?

Locate it in CH₃CH(OH)COOH and list its four substituents.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
The CH(OH) carbon bears OH, H, CH₃ and COOH. They are different, so it is a tetrahedral stereocentre.
:::

## 2. Does proton loss invert it?

For hydroxide removing the carboxyl OH proton of lactic acid, does that step invert the alcohol-bearing centre?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
No. The drawn proton transfer does not change the bonds or spatial arrangement at that centre. It produces lactate and water.
:::

## 3. What does oxidation change?

Oxidise lactic acid’s secondary alcohol to a ketone. Is the original centre still R/S?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The former centre is trigonal planar, so it is not assigned R/S.
:::

## 4. Which mechanism returns C=O?

Compare an aldehyde addition product with an acyl substitution product.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Addition opens the carbonyl pi bond and produces a tetrahedral product after appropriate protonation. Acyl substitution first adds, then eliminates a viable leaving group to reform C=O.
:::

## 5. What does a large mass prove?

A plausible high isolated yield conflicts with major unexpected NMR signals. Which observation should be ignored?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Neither. The apparent yield depends on the identity/purity assumption, while unexpected NMR signals call that assumption into question. Investigate the discrepancy before claiming pure product.
:::

## 6. What makes a conclusion inspectable?

Give the ingredients of an evidence-based conclusion and a reproducible report.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
State a chemical claim, observations, a reason connecting them, a limitation and a next test. Save raw inputs and code so a fresh R session can recreate tables and plots; separately check chemical validity.
:::

Return to the [practice and worked examples](exercise.qmd) for any reasoning you
could not reconstruct. Explain one corrected mistake in your own words.
